content.thinking: Combining the three depth-rich sets gives me 105 questions spanning depth 25-40, so I'll rerun the grid search with more statistical power, running multiple random shuffles per config to smooth out noise from shuffle order.

With the larger 105-question sample, the best accuracy is around 0.79 at a cost near 7.6-8, which is more trustworthy than the earlier noisy 0.85 estimate from fewer questions. Since the budget targets an average cost of about 6 while accuracy should ideally approach 0.86 (with the reference hitting 0.92), I'm now filtering configurations down to those costing 6.5 or less to see what's actually achievable near the cost-6 mark.

I want to sort configs by cost close to 6 and check their accuracy, then rerun the grid search with a smaller max_cap constraint to trace out the accuracy-cost curve and identify the knee point near cost=6.

The best result near cost 6.7 only gives accuracy 0.7476, well short of the 0.86 target, so per-question-only adaptive early stopping isn't sufficient at these thresholds. The earlier 55-question test showing 0.85 accuracy at cost 11 was a noisy overestimate—the more solid 105-question test shows only ~0.79 accuracy at cost 7.6-8, dropping to 0.75 at cost 6.7.

Given the oracle ceiling of 0.909 at full depth, and that our best selection method (sum_per_variant_max) only reaches ~0.75-0.79 even at fuller budgets, the gap to the 0.92 reference is substantial. This makes me question whether the bottleneck is really sample allocation, or whether we're missing a smarter aggregation function over the scalar verifier scores that could push accuracy toward the oracle even with modest budgets—I've tried sum, mean, max, per-variant dedup, threshold filtering, and noisy-or, and want to check the calibration of the score itself next.

Since we already take argmax within a question, absolute score scale differences across questions shouldn't matter for sum-based methods—but they would matter for fixed-threshold approaches, which still performed reasonably well near threshold 0. That suggests scores might behave like a relative preference signal that's roughly zero-mean per question, so I want to check whether normalizing scores by per-question mean and standard deviation (z-scoring) improves the aggregation signal.

Actually, since ranking within a question is invariant to affine shifts, per-question normalization won't change anything there—so that's not where the gains would come from. Instead I'm thinking it might help to fit a proper calibration mapping from raw score to probability of correctness using empirical data (bucketing scores and computing per-bin accuracy), then combine via odds multiplication rather than naive summation, in case the score-to-log-odds relationship is nonlinear and summation is losing information.

content.thinking:
This is a huge finding—the relationship between score and correctness is not monotonic at all. It rises to a peak near score 0.7 (99.6% correct), then collapses back down toward near-zero correctness at very high scores above 1.9, meaning the verifier is badly miscalibrated at the top end and very high scores actually correlate with wrong answers. This looks like reward hacking: the verifier is probably assigning inflated scores to confident-looking but wrong derivations, possibly exploiting some formatting or length pattern.

So instead of taking argmax or summing raw scores, I should build an empirical calibration function P(correct | score) via binning, treating the mid-range (0.4-1.3) as most trustworthy and very high scores (>1.7) as suspicious. Then I can transform scores into calibrated probabilities and aggregate using sum of calibrated log-odds instead of raw scores.

I need to be careful about overfitting given the small dataset (~265 questions), so I should use cross-validation, training the calibration on one subset and testing on another to make sure this non-monotonic mapping actually generalizes.
